title: Modelling data: start from the screens, not the tables
dek: A data model is only good or bad for the questions it has to answer. Write down what each screen reads and each action writes, then choose tables, documents or wide rows, decide where a fact may be copied, and pick keys that lead straight to the rows.

items: List what the app reads and writes, and how often, before drawing a single table. Every hot query needs a key or an index that leads straight to its rows.
Store each fact once by default. Copy a fact only when a frequent read needs it, and decide who keeps the copy up to date, or that it is a snapshot on purpose.
Tables answer questions you didn't plan for; documents suit screens that show one thing and its parts; wide-row stores scale writes for queries you design the keys around.

body.x: Before any tables, list each screen and action with what it reads or writes and roughly how often. For Zotato, a few of them:

body.x: Each row becomes a query, and each query needs a fast path. A query that the model can only answer by reading everything shows up here, on paper, rather than at 8:30 pm on a Friday.

items: The things with their own identity get a table (or collection) and an ID: customers, restaurants, dishes, orders, riders.
One-to-many: a restaurant has many dishes, so each dish row holds `restaurant_id`. The many side points to the one side.

Many-to-many: an order has many dishes and a dish appears in many orders, so a third table, `order_items`, holds one row per pair, along with what belongs to the pair: the quantity and the price paid.
Use IDs the system makes, not facts about the world. Phone numbers change and get reused by someone else; a customer ID never does.

body.cap: The same order as four linked tables and as one document. Tables store each fact once and join at read time; the document is one read, but it carries copies, and copies don't change when the original does.

body.label: Three shapes of data
head: Shape
How it stores data
Good at
Weak at
rows: Tables (PostgreSQL, MySQL)
Rows in tables, linked by IDs and joined when read
Any question, including ones nobody planned; transactions across tables
Spreading one table over many machines; that needs sharding
Documents (MongoDB)
One nested record per thing, read and written whole
Screens that show one thing and its parts; records whose fields vary
Data shared by many records; questions that cut across documents
Wide rows (Cassandra, DynamoDB)
Rows grouped by a partition key and sorted by a sort key
Very high write rates; known queries at any scale
Questions the keys weren't designed for

body.x: Most designs should start with tables, because a relational database answers questions you didn't plan for and keeps related changes in one transaction. Move to another shape when a specific need, such as the write rate or records that vary a lot, outweighs that, and say what the need is.
Copy a fact only when a read pays for it

body.cap: Working the rating out on every view costs 48,000 rows per view. Keeping it on the restaurant's row costs one row per view and one extra update per review. Reads outnumber reviews by far, so the copy wins.

items: Normalised means each fact lives in one place: the restaurant's name is in `restaurants`, and orders point to it. Updates touch one row, and nothing can disagree.
Denormalised means keeping a copy where it is read: the rating on the restaurant's row, the restaurant's name inside each order document. Reads get cheaper; every write has to update the copies.
Some copies are snapshots and must never be updated. An order keeps the dish name and the price at the time it was placed, even after the menu changes. That is correct, not stale.
Every live copy needs an owner: the same transaction, as with the rating; a background job; or a consumer of change events. A copy nobody owns drifts away from the original.

body.x: Keep the rating as a running sum and count (`rating_sum`, `rating_count`) rather than an average, so a new review adds to both and the average is a division at read time.
In Cassandra or DynamoDB a query has to name the partition it reads, so you design the keys from the queries. One table often serves one query, and the same order may be written twice, in two shapes.

body.label: ZOTATO · ORDERS, KEYED BY THE QUESTION
body.x:
orders_by_customer     partition: customer_id         sort: placed_at, newest first
  # "my orders": one partition, already in order

orders_by_restaurant   partition: restaurant_id, day  sort: placed_at
  # the kitchen screen: one partition per restaurant per day

rider_locations        partition: rider_id            sort: at, newest first
  # "where is my rider": the first row of one partition; rows expire after a day
body.say: Three tables. Orders by customer, partitioned by customer ID and sorted newest first, serves My orders from one partition. Orders by restaurant, partitioned by restaurant ID and day and sorted by time, serves the kitchen screen. Rider locations, partitioned by rider ID and sorted newest first, serves order tracking from the first row; rows expire after a day.

items: Adding the day to the restaurant's partition key stops a busy restaurant's partition from growing forever.
Writing one order to two tables is normal here. It usually goes through a stream of changes, so if one write fails it is retried rather than lost.
A question you didn't design for, such as 'every order for paneer tikka last month', needs a new table or a trip to an analytics store.

body.x: When the model has to change

items: Add, don't rename. Add the new column, write to both, fill in old rows in small batches, switch reads over, and remove the old column in a later release.
Adding a column that may be empty is quick in most databases. Rewriting every row of a big table, or building an index without the online option, can block writes for a long time.
Documents make new fields easy, but old documents keep their old shape. The code that reads them has to handle both, or a background job has to rewrite them.
List the main queries with rough rates before drawing tables, and say which ones are hot.
Start with tables in a relational database unless something pushes you elsewhere; name the something.
For each hot query, point at the key or index that serves it.
When you copy data, say who keeps the copy up to date, or that it is a snapshot on purpose.

body.x: Put a database in a Lab design, click it and open its schema: add orders, order items and restaurants with their keys and indexes. In a problem's practice, the request tests check every query against the schema you wrote.

body.label: Go deeper: one row that everyone writes to

body.x: A count kept on one row works until that row is updated thousands of times a second. Every update waits for the row's lock, so writes queue up behind each other. The like count on a post that goes viral is the classic case.

items: Split the counter into, say, 20 rows, add to a random one, and sum them when reading.
Or count in a cache and write the total to the database every few seconds. The number on screen is then a few seconds behind, which nobody notices on a like button.
